The relative “que” (no accent) is unstressed and runs on: “la app que uso” = “laapqueuso”. “¿Qué?” (question) is stressed.
The same: relative “donde” is soft, the question “¿dónde?” is stressed.
QUE links two sentences and means “that”, “which” or “who”. It works for things AND people, singular AND plural. Super simple!
La tarta que está en la mesa.
The cake that’s on the table.
In English you can often drop “that” (“the app I use”). In Spanish you can NEVER drop QUE: “la aplicación que uso”, never “la aplicación uso”.
The relative “que” has NO accent. “Qué” with an accent is only for questions and exclamations (¿Qué es? ¡Qué bonito!).
When you refer to a place, you use DONDE (where), without an accent:
The shop where I buy bread is closed on Mondays.
You can also use “en el que / en la que”: el pueblo en el que nací. Same meaning.
3. After prepositions: el que, la que, quien
When the relative comes after a preposition (con, de, a, para…), you use ARTICLE + QUE (or QUIEN for people). The preposition always goes in front, never at the end as in English:
El botón con el que enciendes el móvil.
The button you turn the phone on with.
El grupo del que habla tu madre.
The group your mother talks about.
The article agrees with the noun: el botón → con EL que; la casa → en LA que; los amigos → con LOS que (or con quienes).
When you’re not referring to a specific noun but to an idea, you use LO QUE:
What I want is to talk to you all.
I don’t understand what you’re saying.
What I like most about Madrid is the people.
Don’t confuse “¿Qué quieres?” (a question: what do you want?) with “Lo que quiero…” (what I want…). In statements, “what” = LO QUE.

Two months after Lucía’s lesson, Grandma Rosario wrote her first post on a blog for older people.
My name is Rosario, I’m eighty-one and two months ago I got my first mobile phone.
At first I was scared. It was a gadget I didn’t understand.
My granddaughter Lucía, who is very patient, taught me the basics.
Now I use WhatsApp every day. It’s the app I talk to my family with.
What I like most is video calls. I can see my brother Manuel, who lives in Mexico.
I hadn’t seen his face for twenty years. We both cried!
I’ve also discovered recipes on the internet. There’s a website where I find all the dishes from my childhood.
But there are things I don’t like. People who look at their phones while they eat, for example.
In my house there’s a rule: there are no phones at the table. What we do is talk.
And some advice for those who are scared of technology: it’s not that hard. You just need someone who teaches you with love.

After learning to use WhatsApp, Grandma Rosario discovered something new: cooking videos on the internet.
She watched them every afternoon, but something bothered her. “These people don’t know how to cook,” she said. “That cocido isn’t a real cocido.”
One Sunday Lucía suggested an idea: “Grandma, why don’t we film a video of you cooking? What you do is what people want to see.”
Rosario laughed. “Me? On the internet? At eighty-one?” But after thinking about it for a while, she agreed.
They filmed the first video in the kitchen on Lucía’s phone. Grandma made her cocido while telling stories from her childhood.
She didn’t follow any script. She made mistakes, laughed, scolded Lucía for not filming properly and gave life advice between recipes.
Lucía uploaded the video to a social network with the title “Grandma Rosario cooks like sixty years ago”. At first only her friends saw it.
But three days later the video had a hundred thousand views. A week later it had a million.
People wrote her messages from all over the world: from Mexico, Argentina, Japan and even Romania.
A girl from Buenos Aires wrote: “You remind me of my grandmother, who died last year. Thank you for making me cry and smile at the same time.”
Now Grandma posts a video every Sunday. She has more followers than all her grandchildren put together.
A cookware company offered her money to advertise their pots, but she said no. “I only use my mother’s pot,” she explains, “and that one isn’t for sale.”
When a journalist asked her what her secret was, Grandma answered: “There’s no secret. I cook with time, with love and without looking at my phone.”
And then, looking at the camera, she added: “Well… except on Sundays.”
Recently Grandma filmed a special video with Kenji. They cooked together: she made the cocido and he made the cocido gyoza.
It was her most-watched video. In the comments someone wrote: “I want to be adopted by this grandma”. Rosario read it and replied: “Come on Sunday. There’s room at the table”.
And that Sunday three followers really did come to lunch. Rosario made cocido for everyone.
